name: Audio and Video Evidence
title: Audio and Video Evidence
answer: Audio and video evidence covers recorded sound and moving images that may be relevant to a legal matter, including body camera footage, surveillance video, voicemail, conference call recordings, deposition recordings, and social media clips. In e-discovery it is treated as electronically stored information, so the same phases apply: identification, preservation, collection, processing, review, and production. The work often involves transcripts, translations, speaker labels, on-screen text, and redactions for privacy or privilege. Because these files are large and time-based, review is usually organized around time ranges, speakers, and events rather than page images.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Audio and video evidence covers recorded sound and moving images that may be relevant to a legal matter, including body camera footage, surveillance video, voicemail, conference call recordings, deposition recordings, and social media clips. In e-discovery it is treated as electronically stored information, so the same phases apply: identification, preservation, collection, processing, review, and production. The work often involves transcripts, translations, speaker labels, on-screen text, and redactions for privacy or privilege. Because these files are large and time-based, review is usually organized around time ranges, speakers, and events rather than page images.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Audio and video evidence runs on storage and compute that can handle large, time-based files, typically object storage, media servers, and review platforms that support playback and annotation. Processing pipelines use transcoding, speech-to-text, speaker diarization, and computer vision for objects, faces, and on-screen text. Some teams keep everything on premises for confidentiality, while others use cloud services with encryption and access controls. Graphics processing units speed up transcription and video analysis, and load files carry metadata and references into review databases.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with collection that preserves the original file, its hash value, and its metadata, often by copying from a device or platform with a documented chain of custody. Analysts then create working copies, transcribe speech, label speakers, translate where needed, and extract text from frames. Reviewers search by keyword, time code, speaker, or visual object, and they mark relevant segments, privilege, and redactions. Quality control checks the transcript against the audio, confirms redactions, and verifies that productions match the review decisions. Authentication may require an expert to explain how the file was captured, stored, and handled.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in audio and video evidence turn on privacy, consent, and provenance. Recording laws vary by jurisdiction, and bystanders, minors, patients, and confidential settings may require redaction or exclusion. Provenance matters because a file can be edited, synthesized, or mislabeled, so hash values, metadata, and audit trails support authentication. AI tools add risk when speech recognition mislabels words, when face or object detection produces false matches, and when generative models create convincing but fake recordings. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, a reminder that training data and synthetic media are contested areas.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward multimodal models that can search speech, sound, and images together, and toward real-time transcription and redaction during review. Provenance standards for media are gaining attention as a way to distinguish captured recordings from generated ones. Deepfake detection and audio forensics are becoming routine parts of authentication challenges. Regulation is expanding, and the site tracks 6,946 state AI bills. Smaller, on-device models may let teams process sensitive recordings without sending them to a third party.
